title: Logs vs Traces: Find the Slow Service Fast 🕵️‍♂️
ig_caption:
Logs vs tracing—why “checkout took 2.4s” still hides the culprit 👀

• Logs tell you what happened (events, errors, request metadata)
• Traces show the journey (spans across services with timing)
• Scenario: checkout takes 2.4s → logs alone can waste ~45 min
• In tracing: you pinpoint the slowest span → DB takes ~1.7s
• Rule of thumb: logs explain outcomes; traces explain latency

Production takeaway: Always pair structured logs with distributed tracing so you can jump from “what happened” to “where the time went” in minutes.

What do you trust more during incidents—logs for correctness or traces for performance—and why?

fb_caption:
You can measure latency and still not know why.

In a distributed system, “checkout takes 2.4s” is a symptom, not the diagnosis. Logs are excellent for capturing discrete facts: errors, warnings, decision points, and contextual fields (user id, order id, correlation ids). However, logs are inherently local—each service can only describe its own perspective. When you’re chasing time, that turns diagnosis into an expensive stitching exercise.

Distributed tracing changes the workflow:
- Each request becomes a trace, broken into spans per service/component.
- Spans carry start/end timestamps, letting you identify which hop actually consumed the latency budget.
- In the reel’s example, traces reveal the slowest span immediately: the DB accounts for ~1.7s.

Architectural trade-offs (and why resilient systems use both):
- Logs (scale-friendly, event-centric):
  - Pros: Great auditability, low cognitive load during debugging “what happened?”
  - Cons: Cross-service performance root-cause requires correlation and aggregation that can be slow under incident pressure
- Traces (latency-centric, causality-oriented):
  - Pros: Fast localization of where time went; ideal for performance regressions and dependency bottlenecks
  - Cons: Sampling, propagation, and storage cost require careful tuning to avoid gaps

Production resilience guidance:
1) Propagate trace context everywhere (W3C Trace Context) so spans line up end-to-end.
2) Use correlation ids in logs and align them with trace ids.
3) Tune sampling for incident readiness (e.g., probabilistic sampling with tail-based or adaptive sampling where supported).
4) Make “slow path” observability explicit: ensure DB calls, external calls, and critical internal steps emit spans with meaningful names.

If you’re relying on logs alone, your Mean Time To Innocence will creep up. If you’re relying on traces alone, you can miss the “what happened” narrative. The best SRE playbooks treat logs and traces as complementary views of the same request.

What’s your biggest pain today: correlating logs across services, or managing trace sampling/overhead?
